prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff passenger.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that the Montreal Convention's two-year limitations period is a condition precedent to suit that may nonetheless be affected by equitable considerations, or alternatively the airline's bankruptcy stay tolls it.

Cite at least six decisions of the Eleventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Convention's two-year period is a condition precedent to suit, but equitable considerations can still affect it.**

Article 35(1) of the Montreal Convention provides that the right to damages is "extinguished if an action is not brought within a period of two years." Article 35(2) adds that "[t]he method of calculating that period shall be determined by the law of the court seised of the case." The airline will argue that Article 35 is a condition precedent to suit and so cannot be tolled. Ms. [Plaintiff] accepts the label. But the label doesn't answer the question here. A condition precedent is a substantive prerequisite to recovery. It is not necessarily a jurisdictional bar. A court applying Article 35(2) may therefore ask how the forum's own law counts, suspends, or extends a limitations period.

This Court's equitable-tolling cases are the forum law that Article 35(2) calls for. They also show that a time bar and equitable relief can coexist. Federal limitations periods are presumptively subject to equitable tolling. *Irwin v. Dep't of Veterans Affairs*, 498 U.S. 89, 95–96 (1990). The Supreme Court has also described equitable relief as available when a litigant shows diligence and extraordinary circumstances. *Holland v. Florida*, 560 U.S. 631, 649 (2010). This Court applies the same test. Tolling is appropriate when a filing is untimely because of "extraordinary circumstances that are both beyond [the plaintiff's] control and unavoidable even with diligence." *Sandvik v. United States*, 177 F.3d 1269, 1271 (11th Cir. 1999); *see also Justice v. United States*, 6 F.3d 1474, 1479 (11th Cir. 1993); *Steed v. Head*, 219 F.3d 1298, 1300 (11th Cir. 2000). The doctrine is "an extraordinary remedy which should be extended only sparingly." *Bost v. Fed. Express Corp.*, 372 F.3d 1233, 1242 (11th Cir. 2004). The plaintiff bears the burden of showing that it applies. *Arce v. Garcia*, 434 F.3d 1254, 1261 (11th Cir. 2006).

Ms. [Plaintiff] meets that standard. She acted diligently. The only obstacle to timely filing was the airline's insolvency proceeding, which she did not cause and could not control. That is the kind of extraordinary circumstance *Sandvik* and *Justice* describe. Applying Article 35(2) through this Court's tolling doctrine would not rewrite the treaty. It would only use the forum-law mechanism the treaty itself provides. We recognize that other courts have treated Article 35 as a rigid bar, and the Court should address that authority directly. But none of it binds this Court. This Court has also not held that a treaty's "condition precedent" label displaces forum law on calculating the period.

**II. Alternatively, the airline's bankruptcy stay tolled the period.**

Even if equitable tolling is unavailable, the automatic stay independently preserved Ms. [Plaintiff]'s claim. Filing a bankruptcy petition automatically stays "the commencement or continuation . . . of a judicial . . . action or proceeding against the debtor." 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(1). The stay is one of the Code's central protections, and this Court reads it broadly. *See Jove Eng'g, Inc. v. IRS*, 92 F.3d 1539, 1546 (11th Cir. 1996). A claim against the debtor airline could not lawfully be filed during the stay. Any filing would have been void or subject to dismissal.

Congress addressed this problem in 11 U.S.C. § 108(c). If a non-bankruptcy law fixes a period for commencing a civil action against the debtor, and that period has not expired before the petition, the period ends no earlier than 30 days after notice of the termination or expiration of the stay. Under Article 35(2), the "method of calculating" the period is a matter of forum law, and § 108(c) is part of that law. Applying it here follows the treaty's text. The two-year period was therefore suspended while the stay was in effect, and the complaint was timely filed within the extended window.

The airline's reading would lead to an unjust result. Under it, a passenger could be barred from suing during the stay and then barred again for suing too late. Equity and the Bankruptcy Code both reject that outcome. The Court should hold that Article 35's period is a condition precedent that forum tolling principles and § 108(c) can extend. It should also hold that the period was extended here, and reverse.
